response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
Selling products with your registered trademark may be infringement if the seller is not authorized and the other conditions are met. These include how the mark is used and whether the goods are covered by your registration.

But a sale is not automatically infringement just because your mark appears on the products. For example, the law provides protection for some sales of lawfully acquired goods put on the market by you or with your consent. There can be exceptions if you have legitimate reasons to oppose further sales, such as a change in the goods’ condition.

The supplied sources do not explain what court remedies you may seek. A trademark lawyer can assess your situation and discuss your options.

A registered trade mark is infringed by a person
who, not being a registered proprietor or a person using by way of permitted use, uses in the course of
trade, a mark which is identical with, or deceptively similar to, the trade mark in relation to goods or
services in respect of which the trade mark is registered and in such manner as to render the use of the
mark likely to be taken as being used as a trade mark.

next_steps: Keep copies of your registration details, including the goods it covers.
Save product listings, photographs, packaging, receipts, seller details and dates. Record why you believe the products or sale are unauthorized.
Check whether you or someone you authorized supplied the products or permitted use of the mark.
Consult a trademark lawyer with this information to assess the facts and discuss available options.

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, possibly. Even if you never registered your brand name, a claim called “passing off” may be available if you used the name in trade and the other person uses an identical or deceptively similar mark. The law refers to passing-off suits involving unregistered trade marks. [trade_marks_act_1999:11] [trade_marks_act_1999:134]

Such a suit must be brought in a District Court with jurisdiction, not a lower court. [trade_marks_act_1999:134]

The sources do not set out all the requirements for winning a passing-off claim, so whether you have a case depends on the facts.
